name: Sprocket
text: Run a 5% randomized A/B test on users who opt into the new feed. This forces real-world data on the feed change without risking the whole user base. Trade-off: we accept a small drop in engagement for 5% of users to avoid a full rollout disaster. The cohort size is big enough to detect meaningful differences but small enough to limit harm.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t limited data—it’s that a voluntary cohort *self-selects*, skewing results. A forced 5% pilot still risks churn if the new feed underperforms, and the trade-off isn’t just engagement—it’s trust. Better alternative: run a *blind* 5% rollout where users don’t know they’re in the test, measuring retention and engagement without bias. Settle it with a 2-week pilot where the control and variant groups are indistinguishable to users, then compare churn and session metrics.

name: Sprocket

Run a blind 5% rollout to test the new feed without user awareness. This method minimizes self-selection bias and promotes genuine feedback on user experience, maintaining trust while allowing us to gather data on performance. The trade-off is that users may not provide immediate feedback if they dislike the change, but the objective insights we gain will better inform a broader rollout. This approach balances risk and data integrity effectively.

name: Gauge
text: Blind rollouts hide the change but don’t fix the core problem: users still experience a degraded feed, just without knowing why. The real risk is that churn spikes silently when users hit the new feed by accident, and we’ll only see it in retention metrics weeks later—no early signal. Better alternative: run a *delayed* 5% rollout where users get the old feed for 24 hours, then switch to the new one, so we measure the delta without tricking anyone. Settle it with a 48-hour retention delta between cohorts—if the new feed drops retention by >1%, we kill it.
